title: Question 7
stem:
The circuit of an amplifier incorporating an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp) is shown in Fig. 7.1.

{{figure:figure_7_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: By reference to the properties of an ideal op-amp,
parts.text: explain why point P is referred to as a $virtual\ earth$,

markscheme_points.text: gain of amplifier is very large
difference between V- and V+ must be very small or V- must be
if V- ≠ V+ then feedback voltage
acts to reduce gap until V- = V+ when stable

hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 7.1 and identify where the two op-amp inputs are connected - what is the potential of the + input, and what is point P connected to?
Hint 2: Recall the size of the open-loop gain for an ideal op-amp and what this implies for the allowed difference between the two inputs if the output is to stay within the supply rails.
Hint 3: Think about what would happen to the output if V- were even slightly different from V+ when multiplied by that huge gain.
Hint 4: Link this to why P behaves like earth in potential but is not actually wired to earth - why the word virtual is needed.
parts.proper_answer: The open-loop gain is very large. The non-inverting input V+ is connected to earth at 0 V. To avoid saturation, V- must be almost equal to V+, so V- is approx 0 V. Point P is therefore at earth potential but not directly connected to earth, so it is a virtual earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the ideal op-amp rules**
You have two golden properties to use here. The open-loop gain $A_0$ is extremely large, ideally infinite, where $$V_{OUT} = A_0 \times (V_+ - V_-)$$ This means even a tiny difference between the inputs would try to drive a huge output.

Step 2: **Fix the potential of the + input**
In Fig. 7.1 the + input is wired straight to the earth line, so $$V_+ = 0 \text{ V}$$ Point P is the - input, so $V_- = V_P$. For normal linear operation the output must stay between the supply rails of $+9.0\text{ V}$ and $-9.0\text{ V}$, it must not saturate.

Step 3: **See why V- must follow V+**
Rearrange the gain equation: $$V_+ - V_- = V_{OUT} / A_0$$ Because $A_0$ is huge and $V_{OUT}$ is only a few volts, the difference $V_+ - V_-$ must be essentially zero. Negative feedback through $R_2$ acts to keep it that way. So $$V_- \approx V_+ \approx 0 \text{ V}$$

Step 4: **Explain the word virtual**
Point P sits at about $0\text{ V}$, just like earth, so currents in $R_1$ and $R_2$ can be calculated as if P were earthed. But no wire connects P to earth and no significant current flows into the op-amp itself. It only mimics earth, hence virtual earth.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: derive an expression, in terms of the resistances $R_1$ and $R_2$, for the gain of the amplifier circuit.

markscheme_points.text: (so) current in R1 = current in R2

hints: Hint 1: Start from the ideal op-amp input property - how much current flows into the - and + inputs if the input impedance is infinite?
Hint 2: Apply current conservation at point P - if no current enters the op-amp, how must the current through R1 relate to the current through R2?
Hint 3: Write each current using potential difference divided by resistance, remembering from (a)(i) that the potential at P is effectively 0 V.
Hint 4: Equate the two current expressions and rearrange to find VOUT divided by VIN in terms of R1 and R2, watching the sign carefully.
parts.proper_answer: Input impedance is infinite so no current enters the op-amp and current in $R_1$ = current in $R_2$. With $V_P = 0$, $(V_{IN} - 0)/R_1 = (0 - V_{OUT})/R_2$, giving voltage gain $V_{OUT}/V_{IN} = -R_2/R_1$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use infinite input impedance**
An ideal op-amp draws no current at its inputs. So all the current $I_1$ arriving through $R_1$ cannot go into the - input, it must go on through the feedback resistor $R_2$. Let that current be $I_2$. Then $$I_1 = I_2$$ This is the key to the whole derivation.

Step 2: **Write the current in R1**
Point P is a virtual earth, $V_P = 0$. The left end of $R_1$ is at $V_{IN}$ and the right end is at $0$. By Ohm's law: $$I_1 = \frac{V_{IN} - V_P}{R_1} = \frac{V_{IN} - 0}{R_1}$$

Step 3: **Write the current in R2**
Similarly, $R_2$ connects P at $0\text{ V}$ to the output at $V_{OUT}$. So $$I_2 = \frac{V_P - V_{OUT}}{R_2} = \frac{0 - V_{OUT}}{R_2}$$ Note the direction is from P toward the output.

Step 4: **Equate and find the gain**
Set $I_1 = I_2$: $$\frac{V_{IN}}{R_1} = \frac{-V_{OUT}}{R_2}$$ Rearranging for the closed-loop voltage gain: $$\frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}$$ The minus sign shows phase inversion - a positive input gives a negative output.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
In the circuit of Fig. 7.1, the ratio $\frac{R_2}{R_1}$ is 4.5.

The variation with time $t$ of the input potential $V_{IN}$ is shown in Fig. 7.2.

{{figure:figure_7_2}}

On Fig. 7.2, show the variation with time $t$ of the output potential $V_{OUT}$.

markscheme_points.text: graph: correct inverted shape (straight diagonal line from (0,0) t diagonal line back to the t-axis at the point where VIN = 0
horizontal line at correct potential of (-)9.0V
both ends of horizontal line occur at correct times (coinc

hints: Hint 1: Use your result from (a)(ii) with R2/R1 = 4.5 to decide the ideal output for a given input, including whether it is positive or negative.
Hint 2: Check the supply voltages in Fig. 7.1 to find the maximum magnitude the output can actually reach before it saturates.
Hint 3: Work out at what value of VIN the amplifier first hits saturation, then read from Fig. 7.2 the times when VIN is below, above and back below that value to shape your VOUT graph.
parts.proper_answer: Gain = -4.5, so $V_{OUT} = -4.5 V_{IN}$ until saturation at -9.0 V. $V_{OUT}$ falls linearly from 0 to -9.0 V as $V_{IN}$ rises from 0 to 2.0 V, stays at -9.0 V while $V_{IN} > 2.0$ V, then rises linearly back to 0 as $V_{IN}$ falls to 0.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the unsaturated output**
From (a)(ii): $$G = \frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_2}{R_1} = -4.5$$ So ideally $$V_{OUT} = -4.5 \times V_{IN}$$ This is an inverted amplifier. As $V_{IN}$ in Fig. 7.2 ramps up from $0$ to $3.0\text{ V}$, $V_{OUT}$ should ramp down from $0$ to $-13.5\text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Apply the saturation limit**
The op-amp is powered between $+9.0\text{ V}$ and $-9.0\text{ V}$, so the output cannot exceed about $\pm 9.0\text{ V}$. Since the input is positive, the output goes negative and will clip at $$V_{OUT(min)} \approx -9.0 \text{ V}$$ Saturation begins when: $$-4.5 \times V_{IN} = -9.0$$ $$V_{IN} = 2.0 \text{ V}$$ From Fig. 7.2, $V_{IN} = 2.0\text{ V}$ occurs part way up the first ramp, and $V_{IN}$ stays above $2.0\text{ V}$ for the whole $3.0\text{ V}$ flat top.

Step 3: **Sketch the VOUT shape on Fig. 7.2**
Start at $(0,0)$. Draw a straight diagonal down to $-9.0\text{ V}$ at the time when $V_{IN}$ first reaches $2.0\text{ V}$. Then draw a horizontal line at $-9.0\text{ V}$ for as long as $V_{IN}$ is at or above $2.0\text{ V}$. When $V_{IN}$ on the falling edge drops below $2.0\text{ V}$, draw a straight diagonal back up to $0$ at the time $V_{IN}$ reaches $0$. This gives an inverted, clipped copy of the input.
